title: Variance decomposition of 'site shift' into scanner, protocol, demographics, and annotation-convention components.
problem: Known: 'multi-site degradation' is reported as a single number; sites differ simultaneously in hardware, protocol, population, and labeling conventions, so the term explains nothing actionable.
hypothesis: In a matched-cohort design on multi-center cardiac MRI (M&Ms) and pathology (CAMELYON17), annotation-convention plus population components jointly explain more of the cross-site performance variance than scanner hardware, contradicting the community's scanner-centric framing.
why_important: Harmonization investments (scanner-side vs label-side) currently allocate blind; a variance budget tells the field where the money should go.
why_novel: Multi-site papers report gaps; none publish a formal variance decomposition with matched cohorts isolating each factor.
minimal_experiment: On M&Ms (vendor and center labels available), fit mixed-effects models of per-case Dice with vendor/center/pathology covariates; on CAMELYON17 use center labels; report variance shares with bootstrap CIs.
main_risk: Factors are partially confounded in observational data; matched subsampling shrinks effective n.
survival_note: Flagship candidate for the cluster; everything else in B2 hangs off this decomposition.

title: Feature-space divergence metrics do not predict medical performance drop: a falsification study of shift 'distances'.
problem: Known: MMD/FID/Frechet-style distances between feature distributions are widely used to quantify domain shift and select adaptation strategies; their predictive validity for segmentation degradation is assumed, not shown.
hypothesis: Across many site pairs, feature-space divergence correlates weakly (rho < 0.3) with actual Dice drop because task-relevant shift lives in a low-dimensional subspace that generic divergences dilute; a divergence restricted to decision-relevant directions predicts far better.
why_important: If generic distances are uninformative, dozens of shift-quantification papers and deployment monitors built on them are unfounded.
why_novel: Correlation between shift metrics and classification accuracy exists for natural images; the segmentation/medical version, and the subspace-restricted contrast, do not.
minimal_experiment: Compute 6 divergence measures between all site pairs in M&Ms/CAMELYON17/PolypGen; correlate with cross-site Dice drops of fixed models; compare against divergence in gradient-aligned subspaces.
main_risk: Limited number of site pairs bounds statistical power; aggregate across 3 datasets.
survival_note: Keep; negative result would be widely cited.
suspected_published: possibly - accuracy-prediction-under-shift literature exists for classification; dense medical version seems open

title: Scanner identity is linearly decodable from FM features; does removing it help or hurt segmentation?
problem: Known: features from medical images encode acquisition fingerprints; harmonization methods assume removing them improves generalization, but scanner-correlated features may carry task signal.
hypothesis: Linear scanner-identity decodability from FM features is near-ceiling, yet projecting out the scanner-discriminative subspace changes cross-site segmentation by less than 1 Dice point - the fingerprint is real but task-orthogonal, falsifying the core premise of feature-level harmonization.
why_important: A large harmonization literature assumes fingerprint removal is the mechanism of improvement; testing the premise directly could redirect it.
why_novel: Fingerprint decodability and harmonization are studied separately; the orthogonality test connecting them is missing.
minimal_experiment: Train scanner probes on FM features from M&Ms/CAMELYON17; remove discriminative subspace (INLP-style projection); measure cross-site segmentation before/after with frozen decoder.
main_risk: Linear removal may not capture nonlinear fingerprint use; complement with nonlinear adversarial probe.
survival_note: Keep; clean falsification design.

title: CT reconstruction kernel is a larger nuisance factor than inter-site variation for boundary metrics.
problem: Known: sharp vs soft reconstruction kernels change edge appearance drastically; LIDC-IDRI contains multiple kernels; kernel is rarely modeled in robustness studies.
hypothesis: Within-site kernel change (soft to sharp) degrades boundary F-score and HD95 of segmentation models more than switching sites at matched kernel, i.e., a hidden within-site factor exceeds the celebrated between-site factor for boundary quality.
why_important: Deployment monitors track site changes but not kernel changes visible in DICOM headers; a cheap header check might beat expensive drift detectors.
why_novel: Kernel effects are known in radiomics; their comparative magnitude against site shift for segmentation is unquantified.
minimal_experiment: Stratify LIDC-IDRI by kernel and site; evaluate fixed models across kernel-vs-site contrasts on nodule boundaries; two-factor analysis; validate on re-reconstructed Mayo LDCT pairs.
main_risk: Kernel and site partly confounded in LIDC; the Mayo paired data mitigates this.
survival_note: Keep; concrete and immediately actionable finding either way.

title: Is MRI sequence shift compositional? Testing whether T1->FLAIR transfer is predictable from T1->T2 and T2->FLAIR.
problem: Known: cross-sequence generalization is studied pairwise; whether sequence shifts compose (forming a predictable geometry over acquisition space) is unknown.
hypothesis: Performance drops across MRI sequence pairs approximately satisfy a metric-like composition (drop(A->C) is predictable within 20% relative error from drops A->B, B->C), implying a low-dimensional acquisition manifold that would let labs predict unseen transfer without running it. (Speculation: composition may fail asymmetrically for contrast-inverting pairs.)
why_important: A predictive geometry of shift would replace exhaustive pairwise benchmarking with interpolation - a large practical saving and a conceptual advance.
why_novel: Nobody has tested algebraic structure of shift; shift is treated as unstructured.
minimal_experiment: On BraTS (4 sequences, same patients), train per-sequence models, evaluate all 12 transfer directions, test compositionality and symmetry of the drop matrix; repeat with FM fine-tunes.
main_risk: Same-patient multi-sequence data makes this clean, but conclusions may not extend to cross-vendor sequence variants.
survival_note: High-concept; keep, it is cheap to falsify.

title: Vendor post-processing, not physics, dominates ultrasound domain shift: a probe using paired raw/processed data.
problem: Known: US vendors apply proprietary speckle reduction and edge enhancement; models trained on one vendor's processed images fail on another's, usually blamed on probe physics.
hypothesis: Models trained and tested across vendor post-processing settings (same raw signal, different processing) lose most of the cross-vendor gap observed in the wild, demonstrating that reversible software processing, not acquisition physics, is the primary shift source in US segmentation.
why_important: If software dominates, shift is fixable at the source (export raw / standardized processing) - a policy fix, not an ML fix.
why_novel: The raw-vs-processed decomposition for US segmentation shift has not been done; requires paired data that a few open platforms (e.g., research US systems) can provide.
minimal_experiment: Use open raw-US platforms (PICMUS/CUBDL beamforming challenge data) to render the same acquisitions under multiple processing pipelines; train/test across processing conditions; compare gap to published cross-vendor gaps.
main_risk: Open raw US with segmentation targets is scarce; may need phantom + limited in-vivo data.
datasets: PICMUS, CUBDL (public raw US); CAMUS for reference (public)
survival_note: Keep if raw-data route is workable; otherwise demote.

title: Stain normalization solves less than believed: re-decomposing pathology site shift into stain, scanner, and lab-procedure parts.
problem: Known: stain normalization is the default answer to pathology domain shift, yet cross-center failures persist after normalization; the residual is unattributed.
hypothesis: After state-of-art stain normalization, the majority of the residual cross-center gap on CAMELYON17 is attributable to scanner optics and tissue-processing (sectioning/fixation) factors, measurable via center pairs sharing stain protocols but differing in scanner.
why_important: The community keeps optimizing the stain axis; quantifying the residual budget stops over-investment in a partially solved sub-problem.
why_novel: Ablation of normalization exists; attribution of the residual to named non-stain factors does not.
minimal_experiment: On CAMELYON17 and PANDA (center metadata), apply strong normalization; regress residual per-center performance on scanner model and lab covariates; complement with a small same-slide-two-scanners set if obtainable.
main_risk: Center metadata granularity may be insufficient; same-slide-rescanned public data is rare.
survival_note: Keep; pathology-FM groups need exactly this number.
suspected_published: possibly - stain-vs-scanner discussions exist; quantitative residual attribution seems open

title: Prevalence shift corrupts self-training and fine-tuning of segmentation models independently of covariate shift.
problem: Known: sites differ in disease prevalence and severity mix; adaptation methods consume unlabeled target data whose label distribution differs, but segmentation work conflates this with appearance shift.
hypothesis: Holding appearance fixed (same site, resampled prevalence), self-training-based adaptation degrades monotonically with prevalence mismatch and can end below the unadapted baseline - prevalence shift alone breaks adaptation, without any covariate shift.
why_important: Identifies a failure mode of the most popular adaptation family that no amount of appearance harmonization fixes.
why_novel: Label-shift theory exists for classification; its clean experimental isolation for dense medical adaptation is missing.
minimal_experiment: On KiTS/LiTS, construct target pools with controlled lesion-prevalence ratios by resampling cases; run standard self-training adaptation; plot adapted performance vs prevalence mismatch.
main_risk: Resampling reduces target-set size; replicate across seeds to control variance.
survival_note: Strong; clean causal design using only resampling.

title: A 'shift ladder' benchmark built from phantom re-acquisitions: isolating single acquisition factors with physical controls.
problem: Known: no existing benchmark isolates one acquisition factor at a time; observational multi-site data confounds everything; phantoms are dismissed as unrealistic but are the only physically controlled instruments available.
hypothesis: A phantom-based ladder (same object; vary one of dose/kernel/field-strength/coil/vendor per rung) yields per-factor sensitivity profiles of segmentation models that rank-order the factors consistently with in-vivo observational estimates - validating cheap phantom audits as proxies for expensive multi-site studies.
why_important: If phantom sensitivity profiles transfer, any lab can audit robustness for the cost of scanner time instead of multi-hospital consortia.
why_novel: Phantoms are standard in physics QA but essentially unused for learning-based segmentation robustness metrology.
minimal_experiment: Use public phantom collections (e.g., ACR phantom scans, multi-vendor QA repositories) plus one anthropomorphic phantom re-scanned under factor sweeps; evaluate models per rung; compare factor ranking against M&Ms/LIDC observational estimates.
main_risk: Anthropomorphic phantoms lack pathology and soft-tissue realism; transfer validation may fail (which is itself a result).
compute: 1 GPU + scanner access for new phantom sweeps
datasets: Public QA phantom sets; new phantom acquisitions (small)
survival_note: Keep; metrology framing is distinctive, needs scanner access.

title: Body habitus, not hospital, drives abdominal CT segmentation drop: demographic decomposition using metadata-rich public data.
problem: Known: BMI changes fat contrast, organ compression, and noise; site comparisons rarely adjust for population habitus differences.
hypothesis: Conditioning on a habitus index (waist-area fat fraction estimated from the image), the cross-site gap on abdominal organ segmentation shrinks by half or more; the field is partly misattributing demographic composition effects to 'site'.
why_important: Mislabeled causes produce useless fixes (scanner harmonization cannot fix demographics); also raises fairness questions for under- and over-weight patients.
why_novel: Fairness work covers classification and skin tone; habitus-conditioned segmentation analysis on CT is missing.
minimal_experiment: Estimate habitus covariates directly from images in AMOS22/TotalSegmentator/FLARE; fit performance models with site and habitus; report adjusted vs unadjusted site gaps and habitus-stratified accuracy.
main_risk: Habitus estimation from images entangles with the segmentation quality being studied; use independent robust estimators.
survival_note: Strong; fairness + robustness in one cheap study.

title: Does model scale close scanner shift but not convention shift? A double dissociation test for medical FMs.
problem: Known: 'scale fixes robustness' is claimed from natural-image evidence; medical shift includes annotation-convention components that scale plausibly cannot fix.
hypothesis: Across FM sizes, scanner/protocol-induced degradation shrinks with scale, while convention-induced degradation (measured on structures with documented labeling conflicts) is scale-invariant - a double dissociation separating perceptual from label-space robustness.
why_important: Would define which robustness problems justify bigger models versus better label governance - a first-order resource-allocation question.
why_novel: Scale-robustness curves exist for corruption benchmarks; splitting shift into perceptual vs label-space components across scale is new.
minimal_experiment: Evaluate 3-4 sizes of one FM family on (a) M&Ms vendor splits, (b) convention-conflict structures across BTCV/AMOS/TotalSegmentator; plot both degradations vs scale.
main_risk: Few medical FM families expose clean size ladders; may need to rely on general FMs (SAM/DINOv2 ladders) with medical decoders.
survival_note: Flagship-quality question; keep.

title: Scanner software upgrades create step-change performance drift invisible to site-level monitoring.
problem: Known: hospitals upgrade scanner software mid-deployment; longitudinal public datasets rarely expose this, so the effect size is unknown.
hypothesis: In longitudinal collections with acquisition-date and software-version metadata, segmentation performance exhibits detectable step changes aligned with version transitions, with magnitude comparable to cross-vendor gaps for some organ/metric combinations.
why_important: Regulatory monitoring assumes gradual drift; step changes require different detection machinery and vendor-disclosure policy.
why_novel: Software version as a shift variable is almost never analyzed; DICOM headers make it retrospectively accessible.
minimal_experiment: Mine TCIA longitudinal collections (e.g., OAI knee MRI, longitudinal CT screening trials like NLST) for software-version transitions; run fixed models across eras; changepoint analysis on performance and on prediction statistics.
main_risk: GT may not exist across all eras; can substitute prediction-distribution changepoints validated on labeled subsets.
datasets: NLST, OAI, TCIA longitudinal sets (public with registration)
survival_note: Keep; deployment-relevant and data exists.

title: DICOM header metadata predicts model failure better than image-derived features: the cheapest possible failure forecaster.
problem: Known: failure prediction research builds image-level uncertainty estimators; headers already encode protocol, kernel, dose, vendor, thickness - the very factors driving shift.
hypothesis: A gradient-boosted model on header fields alone predicts per-case segmentation failure (Dice below threshold) with AUROC within 0.05 of image-feature-based predictors, at essentially zero compute - and combining both shows headers carry non-redundant signal.
why_important: A free, auditable failure flag deployable in any PACS; also quantifies how much 'shift' is header-visible.
why_novel: Nobody has benchmarked header-only failure prediction against learned uncertainty for segmentation.
minimal_experiment: Across pooled public CT sets with heterogeneous headers (AMOS, FLARE, TotalSegmentator, LIDC), train header-based failure predictors for 3 models; compare AUROC/PR against TTA-variance and confidence baselines.
main_risk: Public datasets partially strip headers; effect may be underestimated relative to hospital reality.
survival_note: Strong; practical, cheap, likely to work.

title: 1.5T-vs-3T is a smaller shift than intra-vendor coil/protocol variation: testing a folk assumption about MRI field strength.
problem: Known: field strength is the headline MRI covariate in robustness discussions; coil arrays and local protocol tweaks vary silently within field strengths.
hypothesis: For brain and cardiac segmentation, the performance gap across field strengths at matched protocol is smaller than the gap across coil/protocol variants at matched field strength - the community monitors the wrong variable.
why_important: Deployment risk models and data-collection strategies key on field strength; redirecting attention to protocol-level covariates changes both.
why_novel: Field-strength comparisons exist in isolation; the head-to-head against within-field protocol variance is missing.
minimal_experiment: Use collections spanning field strengths with protocol metadata (OASIS-3, IXI, M&Ms, ADNI); fit performance models with field/protocol/coil covariates; compare component magnitudes.
main_risk: Coil metadata often incomplete; may need proxy covariates (SNR maps).
survival_note: Keep; myth-testing studies age well.

title: Image harmonization improves appearance metrics while degrading boundary fidelity: a systematic harm audit.
problem: Known: harmonization (histogram matching, style transfer, CycleGAN-like translation) is validated with appearance/FID-style metrics and average Dice; boundary-level and lesion-level harms are rarely audited.
hypothesis: Across standard harmonization families, average Dice gains coexist with measurable boundary displacement and small-lesion erasure on a nontrivial fraction of cases - harmonization trades tail risk for mean performance, which current reporting hides.
why_important: Harmonization is entering clinical pipelines; unreported lesion erasure is a direct safety issue.
why_novel: Individual anecdotes of GAN hallucination exist (known); a quantified harm-vs-gain audit across harmonization families for segmentation is missing.
minimal_experiment: Apply 4 harmonization methods to cross-site pairs (M&Ms, CrossMoDA, MSSEG); measure mean Dice change vs per-case worst-case boundary shift and lesion-recall change; report harm-gain scatter.
main_risk: Harm findings depend on harmonization tuning quality; use published configs faithfully.
survival_note: Strong; safety framing plus negative-result value.
suspected_published: possibly - GAN-hallucination in translation is documented; the systematic seg-harm audit seems open

title: A taxonomy of test-time adaptation failure conditioned on shift type: TTA methods flip from helpful to harmful predictably.
problem: Known: TTA (entropy minimization, BN-stat updates, self-training variants) is benchmark-validated on style-like corruption shifts; hospitals face prevalence, convention, and protocol shifts where TTA can silently hurt.
hypothesis: Each major TTA family has a characteristic failure boundary expressible in shift-taxonomy coordinates (e.g., BN-stat updates help under global intensity shift, hurt under prevalence shift), and the boundary is stable enough across datasets to be used as a deployment decision rule.
why_important: TTA is being deployed as a safety measure; knowing when it becomes the hazard is prerequisite knowledge.
why_novel: TTA benchmarks exist; a shift-type-conditioned failure map for dense medical prediction does not.
minimal_experiment: Construct controlled shift suites (intensity, kernel, prevalence via resampling, convention via cross-dataset labels) on abdominal CT; run 5 TTA methods; build the help/harm matrix with CIs.
main_risk: The matrix could be dataset-specific; validate on a second anatomy (cardiac).
survival_note: Strong; directly consumed by anyone deploying TTA.
suspected_published: possibly - TTA pitfalls papers exist for classification; dense medical shift-conditioned map seems open

title: Calibration collapses before accuracy under progressive shift: an early-warning ordering claim.
problem: Known: models are monitored via accuracy proxies; calibration under shift is studied, but the temporal/dose ordering (which degrades first along a shift continuum) is not established for segmentation.
hypothesis: Along graded shift continua (increasing dose reduction, increasing kernel mismatch, site sequences), pixel- and structure-level calibration error degrades at lower shift doses than Dice does, providing a usable early-warning margin; the ordering holds across architectures. (Falsifiable: find one shift axis where accuracy leads.)
why_important: If calibration is the canary, label-free monitoring gets a principled foundation instead of heuristics.
why_novel: Both quantities are measured under shift, but the lead-lag structure along controlled shift doses is unexamined for dense prediction.
minimal_experiment: Create graded shift ladders (simulated dose/noise/kernel on Mayo LDCT; site-ordinal sequences on M&Ms); track Dice and calibration metrics vs dose; estimate lead margins.
main_risk: Calibration estimation needs labels too in the naive form; pair with label-free calibration proxies to make it deployable.
survival_note: Keep; crisp ordering hypothesis, either outcome informative.

title: Privacy preprocessing is a shift source: defacing, skull-stripping, and cropping measurably change downstream segmentation.
problem: Known: public datasets undergo privacy transforms (defacing MRI, pixel-region removal) that hospital data does not; models trained on public data deploy onto un-defaced images.
hypothesis: Models trained on defaced/stripped data show a systematic performance and bias shift when applied to non-defaced images (and vice versa), large enough to matter for structures even far from the face - privacy transforms leak global intensity/registration effects.
why_important: An invisible, universal train-deploy mismatch built into the public-data ecosystem; nobody has priced it.
why_novel: Defacing effects are studied for morphometry pipelines, not for learned segmentation models' transfer.
minimal_experiment: Use datasets available in both defaced and original forms (some OpenNeuro/ADNI arms); train/test across the 2x2 grid; measure performance and boundary-bias differences by distance from modified region.
main_risk: Access to non-defaced counterparts is restricted; may need DUAs.
survival_note: Keep if data access confirmed; otherwise park.

title: Transfer asymmetry between adult and pediatric imaging quantifies directional structure in demographic shift.
problem: Known: transfer is usually reported one-way; whether adult->pediatric is systematically harder than pediatric->adult (per unit of training data) is unknown, and the answer constrains what 'general' pretraining should contain.
hypothesis: Adult->pediatric transfer loses more performance than pediatric->adult at matched source-set size, because adult anatomy is closer to a 'superset' distribution (speculation: developmental states are compressible from adult endpoints but not vice versa).
why_important: Determines whether scarce pediatric data is better spent on pretraining mixtures or fine-tuning, with implications for any demographic-imbalance axis.
why_novel: Directional asymmetry of demographic transfer has not been measured for segmentation.
minimal_experiment: Assemble age-spanning brain MRI (dHCP neonatal, pediatric collections, adult OASIS/IXI); train matched-size models each direction; compare transfer losses; repeat across two structures.
main_risk: Pediatric segmentation GT scarcity limits the matched-size design; brain may be the only feasible organ.
survival_note: Interesting but data-constrained; middle priority.

title: Sites versus samples: the diversity-scale exchange rate for multi-site medical training.
problem: Known: consortia must choose between recruiting more sites or more cases per site; no quantitative exchange rate exists for segmentation.
hypothesis: At fixed total training size, generalization to held-out sites scales roughly logarithmically with number of training sites and saturates near a small site count (order 5-10), defining an empirical exchange rate (k extra sites worth m-fold data per site) that transfers across organ systems. (Falsifiable: no saturation, or organ-specific exchange rates.)
why_important: Directly prices data-collection decisions for every medical AI consortium and FM builder.
why_novel: Scaling laws exist for data volume; the sites to samples exchange rate for dense medical tasks is unmeasured.
minimal_experiment: On M&Ms (6+ centers) and pathology CAMELYON17/PANDA, sweep site-count x per-site-size grids at fixed budget; fit scaling surfaces for held-out-site Dice.
main_risk: Few public datasets have enough sites; the saturation claim may be under-determined - report CIs honestly.
survival_note: Flagship-quality; expensive but decision-grade output.
suspected_published: possibly - site-diversity effects noted qualitatively in FM papers; the quantitative exchange-rate design seems open

title: Which annotation convention did the model learn? Convention-identification probes as a model audit primitive.
problem: Known: models trained on mixed corpora inherit some blend of conflicting label conventions (organ extents, lesion margins); users cannot tell which convention a black-box model follows.
hypothesis: A small probe set of convention-discriminative cases (where conventions maximally disagree) suffices to identify a model's effective convention blend with high reliability, and published FMs occupy measurably different points in convention space despite similar Dice.
why_important: Convention identity determines downstream measurement compatibility (e.g., volumes comparable across models); an audit primitive makes silent incompatibility visible.
why_novel: Convention conflicts are acknowledged; turning them into an identification instrument for auditing trained models is new.
minimal_experiment: Construct discriminative probes from documented convention conflicts across BTCV/AMOS/TotalSegmentator/FLARE; evaluate 6 public models; embed them in convention space; test probe reliability via split-half.
main_risk: Requires careful curation of genuinely convention-discriminative (not just hard) cases.
survival_note: Strong; audit tools have compounding value across the portfolio.

title: Patient-overlap contamination across public medical datasets: a perceptual-hash census.
problem: Known: public datasets are assembled from overlapping institutional archives (TCIA collections feed many challenge sets); cross-dataset evaluation assumes disjoint patients, which may be false.
hypothesis: A perceptual-hashing and metadata-matching census will find non-trivial patient overlap between popular 'independent' train/eval dataset pairs used in medical FM papers, and removing overlaps measurably reduces reported cross-dataset generalization scores.
why_important: Cross-dataset evaluation is the field's generalization currency; contamination would inflate FM claims systematically.
why_novel: Contamination audits exist for web-scraped natural-image corpora; the medical public-dataset ecosystem has never been censused.
minimal_experiment: Hash all volumes/slices of ~15 popular public CT/MRI datasets; cluster near-duplicates; verify candidates by anatomy matching; re-evaluate one FM's cross-dataset table with overlaps removed.
main_risk: Hash false positives on similar anatomy require careful verification; some sets forbid redistribution of derived IDs (publish methodology + counts only).
datasets: BTCV, AMOS22, LiTS, KiTS, MSD, TotalSegmentator, FLARE, TCIA sources (public)
survival_note: High field-hygiene value; findings publishable regardless of direction.

title: FOV and scan-range conventions (arms-up/down, coverage cutoffs) as an unmeasured geometric shift axis.
problem: Known: datasets crop bodies differently (abdomen-only vs whole-body, arms in/out of FOV); models use border context; the geometric convention is a silent covariate.
hypothesis: Synthetic FOV interventions (cropping a whole-body scan to different coverage conventions) change organ segmentation accuracy by margins comparable to moderate intensity shifts, with errors concentrated near cropped borders but extending surprisingly far inward.
why_important: FOV convention differs between every pair of datasets and hospitals; if its effect is large, many reported cross-dataset gaps are partly geometric artifacts.
why_novel: FOV effects are folklore in nnU-Net practice; a controlled intervention study quantifying interior propagation of border effects is missing.
minimal_experiment: Take TotalSegmentator whole-body scans; generate FOV variants matching BTCV/AMOS/FLARE conventions; evaluate fixed models; map error change vs distance from introduced borders.
main_risk: Padding/normalization choices interact; must sweep pipeline variants (ties to 0395).
survival_note: Cheap, clean, and connects to 0395; keep.

title: Slice thickness interacts with lesion size: shift harm is not additive but multiplicative on small targets.
problem: Known: thick slices hurt small-lesion detection; robustness studies report main effects of thickness and lesion size separately, never their interaction surface.
hypothesis: Recall as a function of (lesion diameter / slice thickness) collapses onto a single curve across datasets and models (a dimensionless detectability law), enabling prediction of archive-specific sensitivity from acquisition parameters alone.
why_important: A dimensionless law would let clinical sites predict miss rates for their protocols without local validation studies - a concrete step toward segmentation metrology.
why_novel: Radiology has partial-volume theory; verifying a collapse law empirically for deep models is new.
minimal_experiment: Simulate thickness ladders from thin-slice LiTS/KiTS/MSD-lung volumes; measure lesion recall vs diameter/thickness ratio for 4 models; test curve collapse quality (R^2 of master curve).
main_risk: Simulated slabs approximate scanner physics; validate on native thick-slice subsets where GT exists.
survival_note: Strong; 'physics-style law' framing is memorable and testable.

title: SSL pretraining on mismatched medical corpora can underperform ImageNet transfer: mapping the corpus-mismatch penalty.
problem: Known: 'medical SSL beats ImageNet' is claimed broadly, but the corpus-task match (modality, anatomy, vendor) varies wildly across studies; the mismatch penalty is unquantified.
hypothesis: Under matched compute, SSL pretraining on a mismatched medical corpus (different modality or anatomy than target) underperforms plain ImageNet transfer for a substantial subset of dense targets - medical-ness of pretraining data is not sufficient; proximity is what matters, with a measurable proximity-benefit curve.
why_important: Institutions burn large compute on in-house SSL assuming domain data always helps; a mismatch penalty map prevents waste.
why_novel: Individual comparisons exist (known); a systematic proximity-vs-benefit curve across modality/anatomy grids does not.
minimal_experiment: Pretrain matched-budget SSL models on CT-abdomen, CT-chest, MR-brain, pathology corpora; fine-tune each on 4 dense targets; build the transfer matrix and regress benefit on corpus-target proximity measures.
main_risk: Expensive; SSL recipe quality confounds - fix one recipe and acknowledge scope.
survival_note: Expensive but decision-grade; candidate for consortium-scale execution.
suspected_published: possibly - scattered evidence in transfer-learning studies; the systematic grid seems open

title: Affine feature-space geometry of site shift: sites as linear transforms of each other in FM representation space.
problem: Known: adaptation methods implicitly assume structured shift; whether medical site shift is approximately affine in modern FM feature spaces (which would make cheap closed-form alignment sufficient) is untested.
hypothesis: For FM features of matched anatomy across sites, an affine map (fit on unlabeled data) explains the majority of the between-site feature discrepancy, and closed-form affine alignment recovers most of the cross-site Dice drop for shallow decoders - shift is 'affine-simple' in good representations. (Falsifiable per site pair.)
why_important: If true, heavy adaptation machinery is unnecessary for many deployments; if false, it kills a family of cheap-harmonization hopes with evidence.
why_novel: Linear-mode-connectivity-style geometric analysis has not been applied to medical site shift in FM feature spaces.
minimal_experiment: On M&Ms and CAMELYON17: fit affine maps between site feature distributions (moment matching); measure residual divergence and downstream recovery with frozen decoders; compare against full fine-tuning.
main_risk: Anatomy-content differences between sites contaminate the feature-matching (not pure 'style'); control with matched-pathology subsets.
survival_note: Keep; geometric claims are cheap to test and highly reusable.

title: Retrospective benchmarks overestimate prospective performance even without site change: the time-split penalty.
problem: Known: virtually all public benchmarks use random splits; deployment is a forward-in-time operation; disease mix, protocols, and equipment drift continuously within a single site.
hypothesis: Re-splitting public longitudinal datasets by acquisition date (train early, test late) reduces measured performance relative to random splits by a consistent penalty, and the penalty size predicts published prospective-validation shortfalls.
why_important: Puts a number on the optimism bias of the entire benchmark culture and offers a zero-cost fix (report time-split results).
why_novel: Temporal validation is standard in clinical prediction modeling; its systematic application and penalty quantification for public segmentation datasets is missing.
minimal_experiment: For datasets with acquisition dates (NLST, OAI, some TCIA), train identical models under random vs time splits; tabulate penalties across tasks; compare with documented prospective-study gaps from literature (qualitatively).
main_risk: Date metadata missing or coarse in many sets; restrict to well-dated collections.
survival_note: Strong; cheap policy-changing result.
suspected_published: possibly - temporal-split critiques exist in clinical ML; segmentation-specific quantification seems open

title: Missing-sequence substitution: multi-sequence MRI models degrade nonlinearly when one input is replaced by a near-equivalent variant.
problem: Known: multi-sequence models (BraTS-style 4-channel inputs) assume fixed sequence sets; real archives substitute variants (T2* for SWI, different FLAIR flavors) rather than omitting channels; robustness work studies omission, not substitution.
hypothesis: Substituting a near-equivalent sequence variant degrades performance more than zero-filling the channel in a nontrivial fraction of cases - models treat the channel as a calibrated instrument, and 'almost right' inputs are worse than 'explicitly missing'.
why_important: Substitution is the common clinical reality; if almost-right beats missing is false, input-validation logic in deployed systems must change.
why_novel: Missing-modality robustness is studied; the substitution-vs-omission contrast is unexamined.
minimal_experiment: On BraTS-trained models, replace one channel with variant acquisitions (from other public sets, intensity-matched) vs zero/mean-filling; compare degradation; characterize failure geography.
main_risk: Cross-dataset variant sequences differ in more than sequence type; careful matching needed.
survival_note: Keep; counterintuitive hypothesis with cheap test.

title: Dose reduction is benign but vendor denoising is not: post-processing as the hidden low-dose shift.
problem: Known: low-dose CT robustness is studied via simulated noise; clinical low-dose images additionally pass through vendor denoisers that alter texture statistics in learned, vendor-specific ways.
hypothesis: Segmentation models are substantially more robust to physical dose reduction (simulated projection-domain noise) than to the vendor denoising applied afterward at matched visual quality - the algorithmic layer, not the physics, carries the shift.
why_important: Robustness benchmarks using additive noise measure the wrong thing; procurement decisions about denoising software acquire an ML-safety dimension.
why_novel: Parallels 0406 for US; for CT, the dose-vs-denoiser decomposition using projection data has not been done for segmentation.
minimal_experiment: Use Mayo LDCT projection data to create (a) low-dose FBP and (b) denoised variants (public denoisers as vendor proxies); evaluate fixed segmentation models across arms at matched noise metrics.
main_risk: Public denoisers only approximate vendor products; conclusions carry a proxy caveat.
survival_note: Keep; pairs naturally with 0400 and 0404 as a reconstruction trilogy.

title: The 'general medical FM' interpolates modalities but has no shared anatomy representation: testing representational unification directly.
problem: Known: multi-modality FMs claim unified anatomical understanding; recent evidence (e.g., PET collapse of CT/MR-trained models) suggests per-modality expertise glued together rather than shared anatomy. Fact vs claim needs a direct representational test.
hypothesis: For the same organ across modalities, FM representations do not align in any common subspace beyond what modality-specific decoders explain: cross-modality linear organ decoders transfer near chance, falsifying 'shared anatomical space' claims for current medical FMs.
why_important: The shared-representation claim justifies the entire multimodal-FM program; testing it representationally (not just via task metrics) determines whether the program's premise holds.
why_novel: Task-level cross-modality failures were recently documented; the representational-alignment test (probe transfer across modality at fixed anatomy) has not been run on medical FMs.
minimal_experiment: Extract FM features for matched organs in CT (AMOS), MR (AMOS-MR/CHAOS), and PET-containing sets (autoPET); train organ probes per modality; measure cross-modality probe transfer and subspace alignment (CKA/procrustes).
main_risk: Negative probe transfer can reflect probe design, not representation; use multiple probe families.
survival_note: Strong; tests the field's central premise with cheap tools.
suspected_published: possibly - task-level evidence just emerging (2026 preprints); representational version seems open
